\section{Empirical Validation}
\label{sec:benchmarks}

The Constitutional Enclosure Theorem guarantees that silent decisions
are compile-time errors.  A natural question follows: does the
compile-time guarantee impose a \emph{runtime cost}?  This section
answers that question empirically, over multiple executions, payload
sizes, thread counts, two virtualized platforms, and three persistence
postures---not the single execution of earlier revisions.

% ----------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Methodology.}
Micro-benchmarks use Criterion's \texttt{iter\_batched} discipline with
\texttt{black\_box} on every input crossing an optimization boundary and
a per-iteration seed that makes the hashed context distinct in every
iteration.  Sweep measurements use a harness whose hot path carries no
harness-injected synchronization; percentiles are estimated online with
the $P^2$ algorithm~\cite{jain1985p2}, O(1) memory per quantile,
and are \emph{estimates}, not order statistics---all tables say so.
Each sweep configuration runs five trials; we report medians and the
trial-to-trial coefficient of variation (CV).  Iteration counts are
calibrated per (payload, mode) with the mode's own operation and are
therefore not comparable across modes; cross-mode comparisons use
throughput and within-mode latency.

\paragraph{Hardware and software.}
Two virtualized platforms: an AMD EPYC~9V74 runner with 4~vCPUs and an
Intel Xeon virtual machine with 2~vCPUs, both Linux x86\_64, toolchain
pinned to \texttt{rustc}~1.98.1 via \texttt{rust-toolchain.toml}.
Both platform sweeps are reduced-footprint snapshots (10\,s and 1\,s
wall targets respectively); the 90\,s dedicated-hardware collection
remains due and is tracked in the artifact's evidence manifest.  We
publish these snapshots with their full environment fingerprints
because they are reproducible today; every table cites the exact CSV
that produced it.

% ----------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\paragraph{Construction latency.}
Table~\ref{tab:construction} reports the end-to-end cost of
\texttt{Verdict::new}---BLAKE3 context hashing, authority-signature
verification, HMAC-SHA256 sealing, and allocation---for three context
sizes.  The payload-scaling portion of the curve is the BLAKE3 hashing
cost; the $\approx$5.36\,\textmu s floor is dominated by the two
HMAC-SHA256 computations (token signature verification and integrity
seal) plus the hex encoding of the evidence identifier, each of which
any accountable system must perform.

\input{section5_table1_construction}

\paragraph{Two-platform thread scaling.}
Table~\ref{tab:platforms} (generated from the sweep CSVs) reports the
full pipeline---token construction, sealing, and in-memory persistence
attempt---at 4~KiB payloads while scaling threads.  Median latency is
flat up to the platform's vCPU count (1.72\,\textmu s at one thread on
the EPYC runner, 2.30\,\textmu s at four) with trial CV below 0.5\%,
the empirical signature of the absence of structural lock contention
claimed in Section~\ref{sec:type_system}.

\input{section5_tables_generated}

\paragraph{Five-mode accountability contrast.}
Table~\ref{tab:fivemode} is the honest version of the comparison an
architect actually faces.  Against a status quo that logs the
\emph{complete} context (the only way a non-cryptographic logger
preserves evidentiary value), the durable BTV pipeline is
$11.1\times$ \emph{slower} at 4~KiB.  Against a status quo that logs
only a digest and metadata, the durable BTV pipeline is
$155.5\times$ \emph{slower}---the price of signature verification,
sealing, and a real synchronous write to disk.  The gap between the two
status-quo arms is a design choice of the baseline, not a property of
BTV; we therefore report the pair as a sensitivity range rather than a
single multiplier.  The durable arm's absolute numbers come from a
containerized filesystem and are a lower bound on bare-metal fsync
cost.  \textbf{This inverts an earlier revision's headline claim of
$2.6\times$ \emph{faster} against the full-context baseline}; the
earlier number came from a benchmark defect (next paragraph), and we
report the corrected direction rather than the more flattering one.

\paragraph{Durability is not free---and an earlier number understated
how not free.}
An earlier revision's durable-persistence figure was corrupted by a
harness defect, not by an in-memory database (a prior round's mistake):
the sweep's per-iteration payload nonce was local to a single trial and
thread, so every trial after the
first, and every thread after the first within a trial, replayed the
exact evidence trial 0/thread 0 had already logged.  The append-only
log's idempotency guarantee (Section~\ref{sec:linear_resources}, OS-03)
correctly recognized these as identical replays and returned
\texttt{Ok(())} without a second \texttt{INSERT}---correct behavior for
a caller resubmitting the same evidence, wrong data for a benchmark
that believed every call was new evidence.  Four of every five trials
measured a fast no-op, and the published $10.22\,\textmu$s figure was
that no-op's cost.  The harness now draws every durable-mode payload
from one process-wide atomic counter, so no two calls can ever collide,
and asserts at the end of every run that rows persisted equals
operations issued; this collection passed exactly
(1{,}803{,}460 of 1{,}803{,}460).  The corrected measurement is
$261.44\,\textmu$s median (real file, WAL, full synchronization) per
durably persisted verdict, roughly $33\times$ the in-memory path---not
the $160\times$ previously reported, since that ratio compared a real
number to a corrupted one.  We report the unflattering number because a
defect that makes the accountable path look cheaper than it is defeats
this artifact's purpose as thoroughly as the silent decision it exists
to prevent.

\subsection{Worked Examples}
\label{sec:worked-examples}

Three worked examples demonstrate BTV in semi-realistic scenarios: credit
scoring under LGPD (30-day appeal window), hiring screening under EU AI Act
Art.~86 (high-risk classification), and emergency triage (where \texttt{Allow}
decisions also require evidence).  Each example constructs verdicts from
domain-specific payloads and verifies integrity.  Source code is included in
the companion repository (\texttt{examples/}).
